home.title: Combinatorial Games Visualization
problems.addproperdivisor.title: Add Proper Divisor
problems.addproperdivisor.description: Start with n = 2. Two players A and B move alternately by adding a proper divisor of n to the current n. The goal is a number ≥ 1990. Who wins?
problems.addproperdivisor.helpertext: Select the factor that you want to add
problems.addsmaller.title: Add Smaller Number
problems.addsmaller.description: This game begins with the number 2. In one turn, a player can add to the current number any natural number smaller than it. The player who reaches the number 1000 or more wins. Who has the winning strategy?
problems.addsmaller.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.addsmaller.helpertext: Select the number that you want to add
problems.bachet.title: Bachet's Game
problems.bachet.description: Two players are playing with n rocks. On each turn, one player alternately take 1, 2, or 3 rocks (as long as it is possible). The player that takes the last rock win. Who has the winning strategy for each value of n?
problems.bachet.helpertext: Select how many rocks to be removed
problems.bachet.form.text: Choose a value of n that does not exceed 120
problems.centro22p1.title: Take Out The Sum of The Digits
problems.centro22p1.description: There is a pile with 2022 rocks. Ana and Beto play by turns to the following game, starting with Ana: in each turn, if there are n rocks in the pile, the player can remove S(n) rocks or n-S(n) rocks, where S(n) is the sum of the the digits of n. The person who removes the last rock wins. Determine which of the two players has a winning strategy and describe it.
problems.centro22p1.helpertext: Select how many rocks to be removed
problems.centro22p1.form.text: Choose a value of n that does not exceed 500
problems.ibero11p1.title: 2n, 3n, n+1
problems.ibero11p1.description: The number 2 is written on the board. Ana and Bruno play alternately. Ana begins. Each one, in their turn, replaces the number written by the one obtained by applying exactly one of these operations: multiply the number by 2, multiply the number by 3 or add 1 to the number. The first player to get a number greater than or equal to 2011 wins. Find which of the two players has a winning strategy and describe it.
problems.ibero11p1.helpertext: Select the operation you want to apply
problems.keepcoprime.title: Keep Coprime Numbers
problems.keepcoprime.description: Start with n ≥ 12 successive positive integers. A and B alternately take one integer, until only two integers a and b are left. A wins if gcd(a, b) = 1, and B wins if gcd(a, b) > 1. Who wins?
problems.keepcoprime.helpertext: Select the number to be removed
problems.keepcoprime.form.text: Choose a value of n that does not exceed 120
problems.keepmultiply.title: Keep Multiply
problems.keepmultiply.description: A and B start with p = 1. Then they alternately multiply p by one of the numbers 2 to 9. The winner is the one who first reaches (a) p ≥ 1000, (b) p ≥ 1000000. Who wins, A or B?
problems.keepmultiply.helpertext: Select the number that you want to multiply
problems.lusophon22p2.title: Fruits in a Box
problems.lusophon22p2.description: Anselmo and Claudio are playing alternatively a game with fruits in a box. The box initially has 32 fruits. Anselmo plays first and each turn consists of taking away 1, 2, or 3 fruits from the box or taking away 2/3 of the fruits from the box (this is only possible when the number of the fruits left in the box is a multiple of 3). The player that takes away the last fruit from the box wins. Which of these two players has a winning strategy? How should that player play in order to win?
problems.lusophon22p2.helpertext: Select how many fruits to be removed
problems.movingchip.title: Moving Chip
problems.movingchip.description: Initially there is a chip at the corner of an n × n-chessboard. A and B alternately move the chip one step in any direction. They may not move to a square already visited. The loser is the one who cannot move. (a) Who wins for even n? (b) Who wins for odd n? (c) Who wins if the chip starts on a square, which is neighbor to acorner square?
problems.movingchip.form.text: Choose a value of n between 2 and 15, inclusive
problems.movingking.title: Moving King
problems.movingking.description: A king is placed on square a8 of a chessboard. Players take turns moving the king either downwards, to the right, or along a diagonal going downwards and to the right. The player who places the king on square h1 is the winner.
problems.movingking.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.movingrook.title: Moving Rook
problems.movingrook.description: On a chessboard, a rook stands on square a8. Players take turns moving the rook as many squares as they want, either horizontally to the right or vertically downward. The player who can place the rook on square h1 wins
problems.movingrook.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.placingbishop.title: Placing Bishop
problems.placingbishop.description: Two players take turns placing bishops on the squares of a chessboard, so that they cannot capture each other. (the bishops may be placed on squares of any color). The player who is unable to do this loses.
problems.placingbishop.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.placingking.title: Placing King
problems.placingking.description: Two players take turns placing kings on the squares of a 9 x 9 chessboard, so that no king can capture another. The player who is unable to do this loses.
problems.placingking.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.placingknight.title: Placing Knight
problems.placingknight.description: Two players take turns placing knights on the squares of a chessboard, so that no knight can take another. The player who is unable to do this loses.
problems.placingknight.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.subtractfactorv1.title: Subtract Factor (version 1)
problems.subtractfactorv1.description: Given a number 120. Two players alternately subtract the number with a positive factor of that number. The player that writes 0 lose. Who has the winning strategy?
problems.subtractfactorv1.helpertext: Select the factor that you want to subtract
problems.subtractfactorv2.title: Subtract Factor (version 2)
problems.subtractfactorv2.description: Given a number 120. Two players alternately subtract the number with a positive factor of that number that is not 1 or that number itself. The player that cannot do their turn lose. Who has the winning strategy?
problems.subtractfactorv2.helpertext: Select the factor that you want to subtract
problems.subtractlessthanhalf.title: Subtract Less Than Half
problems.subtractlessthanhalf.descriptio: A box contains 300 matches. Players take turns removing no more than half the matches in the box. The player who cannot move loses.
problems.subtractlessthanhalf.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.subtractlessthanhalf.helpertext: Select the number that you want to subtract
problems.subtractpowerof2.title: Subtract Power of Two
problems.subtractpowerof2.description: This game begins with the number 1000. In one turn, a player can subtract from the current number any natural number less than it which is a power of 2 (note that 1 = 2°). The player who reaches the number 0 wins.
problems.subtractpowerof2.source: Mathematical Circles (Russian Experience) by Dmitri Fomin, Sergey Genkin, Ilia Itenberg
problems.subtractpowerof2.helpertext: Select the number that you want to subtract
